Within this GitHub repository due to size limits, we are unable to provide the .svg files that were used to create the poster in Inkscape, feel free to reach out to the UMGCCC Flow Cytometry Shared Resource email (“flowcore”, “@”, “som.umaryland.edu”) to get a sharable copy.
The code to generate QR codes and extract survey comments in R can be found under the code_poster folder. Actual QR codes generated can be found under outputs folder. Images used that were brought in from other sources can be found in the images folder.


Abstract
A semi-supervised pipeline for a comprehensive and scalable analysis of immune heterogeneity in human samples
David Rach1,2, Nginache Nampota-Nkomba3,4, Godfrey Mvula3, Felix A. Mkandawire3, Osward M. Nyirenda3, Winter A. Okoth5,6, Daniela Franco4, Andrea G. Buchwald5, Franklin R. Toapanta5, Marcelo B. Sztein5, Miriam K. Laufer5, Kirsten E. Lyke5, Cristiana Cairo7.
1 Molecular Microbiology and Immunology Graduate Program, University of Maryland School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD, United States 2 Flow Cytometry Shared Resource, University of Maryland Greenebaum Comprehensive Cancer Center, Baltimore, MD, United States 3 Blantyre Malaria Project, Kamuzu University of Health Sciences, Blantyre, Malawi 4 Graduate Program in Life Sciences, University of Maryland School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD, United States 5 Center for Vaccine Development and Global Health, University of Maryland School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD, United States 6 Geographic Medicine Division, Department of Medicine, University of Maryland School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD, United States 7 Department of Microbiology and Immunology, University of Maryland School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD, United States
Spectral flow cytometry (SFC) holds enormous potential for immune profiling in both breadth and depth. For studies of early life human immunology, where the quantity of biospecimen is limited, SFC may allow for a more thorough interrogation of immune responses following immunization or infection.
The increased number of fluorophores does come with increased uncertainty, affecting the estimation of marker abundance during unmixing. Factors such as additional or varied autofluorescence, non-specific binding or tandem degradation of fluorophores, and increased unmixing-dependent spread due to co-expression of markers on rare subsets, introduce uncertainty when analyzing datasets. Developing systematic bioinformatic methods to distinguish heterogeneity from underlying technical artifacts is critical to the production of interpretable, accurate data using SFC.
Additionally, analysis of complex SFC datasets remains a challenge. Manual gating of pre-determined cell populations of interest risks introducing bias by defaulting to past immunologic assumptions and by design narrows our ability to detect changes in other cell subsets. On the other hand, while existing unsupervised methods may capture a broader picture, it may be difficult to discern findings with biologic relevance.
Studying a cohort of Malawian infants with well-characterized prenatal HIV-exposure, we demonstrate a systematic method of analysis suitable for rare subsets. The cohort consisted of three groups of infants born to women with: A) ART-treated HIV infection and
undetectable viral load since before conception and through pregnancy (HEU-lo); B) HIV infection diagnosed and treated at mid-gestation or later, with high viral load at enrollment (HEU-hi); C) no HIV infection (HU). Cryopreserved cord blood mononuclear cells and longitudinal peripheral blood mononuclear cells collected at 4 and 9-months following routine childhood immunizations were thawed, rested for 6 hours, and stimulated in the presence of purified protein derivative (PPD) or Staphylococcal enterotoxin B (SEB). Cells were stained with a 32-color SFC panel to characterize phenotype, activation-induced markers and cytokine production with same day acquisition using a 5-laser Cytek Aurora.
Following acquisition, we carried out a semi-supervised analysis with a custom pipeline that we implemented in R and Rust. Briefly, we performed quality assurance of unmixing controls using the Luciernaga and PeacoQC R packages, replacing problematic single-colors and/or autofluorescence controls as appropriate before unmixing. Samples were biexponentially transformed and automated gating was implemented using the openCyto and flowMagic R packages. Using the interactive Shiny App in our R package Coereba, the calculated split-points between positive and negative events were visualized for each marker and manually adjusted as needed. Identity columns for the marker expression of individual cells were then generated and appended to the .fcs files.
For select cell populations, all events were concatenated, normalized with CytoNorm v2, clustered with flowSOM, and visualized with PaCMAP. Identity data associated with cells across clusters was retrieved, allowing a comparison between algorithm and manual gating performance. In parallel, cells sorted into clusters on the basis of shared marker identity were analyzed to compare their abundance between exposure groups using existing Bioconductor workflows. This mixed approach allowed us to examine the immune response across timepoints, treatment conditions and exposure groups, enabling an exhaustive, comprehensive and scalable characterization of individual heterogeneity

title: Planning
text:
Slide 1
SFC amazing, whether 20 markers or 60, ability to rapidly acquire millions of cells in minutes. expanding our understanding human immunology, potential for biologica characterization rarer subsets, particularly invaluable for clinical specimens limited biospecimen.


Slide 2
Immense potential, with elephants in the room. Uncertainty ~ marker “abundances”, everything affect, tandem degradagtion, non-speicifc, af variation, coexpression. Caution in attributing to biology what could be technical artefat in these large panels.


Slide 3
While if you are interested in a single cell population, the analysis remains essentially the same, there is one area I have constantly grappled with over my PhD. Namely, if we acquired 7 million cells to characterize 100 of our rare population, what is occuring in the rest of the cells. Especially if for a rare clinical cohort.


Slide 4
Unsupervised analytical methods have often been touted as the solution, but in their current implementation, are they fully leveraging the entirety of our unique datasets? Or are they confined to skimming the surface. Similarly, we cluster, is the statistical test even biologically relavent if three distinct groups of cells ended smooshed together. And if our datasets have MFI batch effects, how reliable would they perform.


Slide 5
Because at the end of the day, when it’s 3 AM, I step back. On a spectrum, our discussions about clusters and metaclusters revolve about where we draw the lines. On one end every cell is in a cluster with itself. On the other everything is in the same cluster.


Slide 6
Every panel, depending on our markers, has an ability to define cell populations that are present up to a certain point. And various groups have previous implementations of trying to corral cells of these phenotypes for biological insight.


Slide 7
At the end of the day, I want to leverage the clearest insight out of my panel. Just like I make my single-color controls each time because I don’t want to spend hours after the fact trying to make things work, I don’t see the point of clustering only to spend hours laboriously re-glue-ing things back together. (too much, tone it back?)


Slide 8
We are working with a cohort of malawian infants, well stratefied HIV and ART exposure.

Cryopreserved
0,4,9 months
Using a 32-fluorophore panel, intranuclear, high AB co-expression markers for cytokines and AIMs.
Rested 6 hours, stimulated w PPD, SEB, w/o golgi for 3, with golgi for 9 hours.
Acquired 5-laser cytek Aurora passed QC



Slide 9

Our analysis pipeline has evolved since our previous papers. Previously mainly FlowJo, increasingly in R, with skeleton elements of Rust taking over performance behind the scenes. However, still traditional cytometrist, so interconversion is critical.
Pre-Unmixing, we are using Luciernaga to screen our unmixing control signatures. Visualizing across time, pinpoint bad controls and remove. Similar approach for which samples are getting beads vs. cells.
Screening with PeacoQC, originally R version, but James Moyihan’s Rust implementation is sweet!
Automated Gating to Cell Subsets: openCyto (mainly mindensity with a lot of gate_range arguments), but also flowMagic (both our own GatingSet implementation, but with sebastianos last update going his route).
Using the old Cytoverse docker container to go from a GatingSet back to FlowJo v.10 workspace to allow for corrections by traditional flow cytometrist.
Coereba: newer R packages. Main idea is on a per-cell basis defining a identity column that encompasses all the manual gated definitions for every marker interest. This then travels and can be used to cross-check assumptions for the dimensionality visualizations
Run openCyto mindensity, check, constrain. We interactively update the placements via a Shiny App. Then Coereba is run
Once column is incorporated, we can normalize. Trying CytoNorm and CyCombine, using a single-donor thaw specimen for each experiment. If anyone has suggestions, open, since so far results have been mixed. Typically applying at the cell node level rather than the whole file.
Point, choosing to either downsample for larger pops, or concatenate entire population.
Dimensionality Viz - UMAP or PaCMAP via Python
Gate on “clusters/islands/pick-your-terminology”, process of CoerebaID incorporation is reversible, and we retrieve/rederrive the proportion cells from each donor that ended up in the area that were positive or negative for each marker.
Likewise, these outputs get incorporated into Bioconductor SummarizedExperiment object, allowing for filtering, renumeration, and passing to downstream statistical analysis packages.
As suspected, not all dimensionality methods are separating down to pure populations when visualized.
However, we can quickly iterate out the marker expression plots for an individual specimen.



Slide 10

Enough to anger both sides of the automated gating vs. unsupervised clustering camps
Strong emphasis at the moment on exploratory data analysis.
No stand at this point on where to draw the clustering continuum
Individual nodes are too noisy for standard tests
Off-target uses are those that are fascinating, more programmatic outputs that not have in typical flow cytometry analysis



Slide 11

Identify freezer burned specimens otherwise would have included.
Overnight staining vs. day of, differential population loss?

title: QR Codes

Setup Code

library(qrcode)


QR_Helper <- function(url, output, filename){

code <- qr_code(url)

TheFileName  <- paste0(filename, ".svg")

StoreHere <- file.path(output, TheFileName)

generate_svg(code, filename = StoreHere)
#plot(code)
}
